newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-PLAYERS STRIKE AVERTED AT WORLD EVENT.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-PLAYERS STRIKE AVERTED AT WORLD EVENT.

text.p: Organisers caved in under a threatened strike by players at the world table tennis championships on Saturday.
While third-round action was taking place at the G-Mex Centre, crisis talks were going on behind the scenes as players found they were barred from watching the showcourts from the spectators' stands.
The ban also extended to umpires and national team delegates.

Belgian Jean-Michel Saive, the 1993 losing finalist and president of the players' union (CCTTP), was one of those turned back by stewards. As Saive approached the foot of the stairs leading to the courtside seats, he was asked to show his identity tag and then prevented from entering.

The tournament organisers said they were under pressure because it had not been possible to increase the centre court seating capacity from 3,700 owing to safety regulations, and the last three days of the tournament have been a sell-out.
"This is a ridiculous situation," Saive said as he arranged a meeting with some of his colleagues.
Sweden's 1991 world champion Jorgen Persson said: "I have never before heard of players being unable to support their team mates. It is disgusting."
After their meeting, the players presented an ultimatum to the sport's governing body, the International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF), threatening strike action if the ban was not removed.
The national teams also sent a letter of protest.
Forced into a corner, the organisers immediately withdrew the ban for Saturday and said 900 extra seats would be found for the last two days of the tournament.
"We can only be satisifed this problem has been solved," Saive said. "We were deadly serious about our threat."
Although the Belgian was successful in gaining access to the spectators' seats, he was shown the exit in the field of competition.
Seeded joint fifth, Saive failed to overcome the elegant sliced defence of Japan's Hiroshi Shibutani, who won the third-round match 18-21 21-16 12-21 21-19 21-12.
The Belgian was the only major third-round casualty.
Defending champion Kong Lingui moved into the last 16 at the expense of ex-compatriot Liu Song, who plays for Argentina, one of 16 countries fielding former Chinese mainland players.

Liu never presented a serious challenge to the world number one, who won 21-10 22-20 21-13. Kong was briefly tested in the second set when Liu fought back to deuce after trailing 18-20, but Kong took the next two points with forehand loops.
The champion's opponent for a place in the quarter-finals is Austria's Werner Schlager, who outlasted Sweden's Peter Karlsson in a five setter.

Second-seeded Swede Jan-Ove Waldner, champion in 1989 and a double losing finalist, beat Yugoslavia's Ilija Lupulescu in straight sets for a fourth-round meeting against one of the joint ninth seeds, Croatian Zoran Primorac.

Another successful former champion was 1993 title-holder Jean-Philippe Gatien of France, who cannot relish his next match against world number six Wang Tao, the only Chinese player to come through the team matches undefeated.

World number four Vladimir Samsonov of Belarus continued to impress by dispatching China's Ma Lin in straight sets, but there was no place in the last 16 for Friday's giantkiller, Aleksandr Karakasevic.

The young Yugoslav, who eliminated China's Olympic gold medalist Liu Guoliang, came down to earth when he lost 21-9 21-17 22-2 to Spain's He Zhi Wen, who used to play on the Chinese national team in the 1980s.
Both the men and women were playing two rounds on Saturday to reach the last eight.
